{"type":"text","timestamp":1793302893505,"sessionID":"ses_e76d1d2d2ffelh9DNVyJU6ANDQ","part":{"id":"prt_1892e935a001b5El0DPbCNCjyw","sessionID":"ses_e76d1d2d2ffelh9DNVyJU6ANDQ","messageID":"msg_1892e707d001YjnOiCFQc6E6h9","type":"text","text":"I wrote one primer pair to `/work/primers.fasta`, with the forward primer first:\n\n```\n>fwd\ntagattagaagaagaattaagaagaagattaacagaaagcaagggcgaggagctgtt\n>rev\nctcatatgtatatctccttcttaaagttaaacaaaattatttcta\n```\n\n- **Edit:** the output plasmid is the input plus a 39-nt insertion (`tagattagaagaagaattaagaagaagattaacagaaa`) directly after `…catatg` at position 215. One primer pair is enough for this, so this is the minimum.\n- **Design:** this is the standard Q5 site-directed mutagenesis layout for an insertion. The forward primer carries the 39-nt insertion as a 5' tail, followed by 18 nt that anneal to the template (`gcaagggcgaggagctg`-side sequence). The reverse primer anneals back-to-back with the forward primer's annealing region and has no overlap with it. It is the reverse complement of the 45 nt upstream of the insertion.\n- **Melting temperatures:** I computed these with `oligotm` using your flags, on the annealing portions only. The forward annealing region is 63.81 °C and the reverse is 63.81 °C. They differ by 0.003 °C, which is inside the 5 °C limit, and both are inside 58–72 °C.\n- **Lengths:** the annealing parts are 18 nt (forward) and 45 nt (reverse), both within 15–45.\n- **Reverse primer length:** the reverse primer has to be that long. Its annealing region sits in a very AT-rich stretch (the T7 promoter and RBS region). It only reaches 58 °C at about 28 nt and matches the forward primer's Tm at 45 nt.\n- **Check:** I inserted the 39-nt sequence into the input in Python, and the result is identical to the output sequence.","time":{"start":1793302893504,"end":1793302893504}}}
